title: Eligible SR&ED Expenditures & Qualifying R&D Costs | FAQ
description: What types of expenses qualify as eligible SR&ED expenditures in Canada? Review our FAQ covering R&D salaries, materials, overhead, and contractors.
summary: Eligible SR&ED expenditures in Canada include salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED, materials consumed or transformed, 80% of arm's-length Canadian contract payments, overhead via the 55% proxy amount or traditional method, and, for property acquired after December 15, 2024, restored capital expenditures. Qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earn a 35% enhanced credit on up to $6 million.

body.text: Eligible SR&ED expenditures in Canada include salaries and wages of employees directly engaged in SR&ED, materials consumed or transformed, 80% of arm's-length Canadian contract payments, overhead via the 55% proxy amount or traditional method, and, for property acquired after December 15, 2024, restored capital expenditures. Qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs earn a 35% enhanced credit on up to $6 million.
Executive Overview of the Canadian R&D Fiscal Architecture

Canada maintains one of the most mature and generously funded fiscal architectures for industrial innovation among Organisation for Economic Co-operation and Development (OECD) jurisdictions, anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program. Supporting more than 24,160 businesses annually, the SR&ED program operates through a dual-mechanism statutory framework codified in the Income Tax Act (Canada), R.S.C. 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.) (the "ITA") and the Income Tax Regulations, C.R.C., c. 945 (the "Regulations"). First, subsection 37(1) of the ITA establishes a dedicated tax deduction pool that permits taxpayers carrying on business in Canada to immediately deduct current and qualifying capital SR&ED expenditures against business income in the taxation year incurred, or to carry those unclaimed deductions forward indefinitely to offset taxable income in future taxation years. Second, section 127 and section 127.1 of the ITA provide an Investment Tax Credit (ITC) ranging from a baseline rate of 15% to an enhanced refundable rate of 35% on qualified SR&ED expenditures.

Between December 2024 and March 2026, the Canadian R&D tax landscape underwent its most significant legislative transformation in over a decade. Following public consultations initiated in early 2024 and policy announcements in the December 16, 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES) and the August 15, 2025 Department of Finance draft legislative proposals, Parliament enacted Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026. Retroactively effective for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 (that is, on or after December 16, 2024), Bill C-15 fundamentally recalibrated the federal SR&ED regime through five interconnected structural reforms. First, the legislation doubled the annual expenditure limit for the enhanced 35% ITC from $3 million to $6 million, thereby expanding the maximum annual federal cash refund on current expenditures from $1.05 million to $2.1 million. Second, Parliament raised the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds for Canadian-controlled private corporations (CCPCs) from the historical $10 million to $50 million corridor to a substantially wider range of $15 million to $75 million. Third, Bill C-15 extended access to the enhanced 35% refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for the first time in the program's history, subject to a three-year average gross revenue phase-out between $15 million and $75 million, while simultaneously permitting CCPCs to elect into this revenue-based phase-out test. Fourth, the statute restored the eligibility of capital expenditures on depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, alongside related lease costs, which had been excluded from the SR&ED regime since January 1, 2014, granting partial ITC refundability at a rate of 40% for enhanced-rate claimants. Fifth, the legislation expanded the prior-year taxable capital ceiling used to compute the "qualifying income limit" for qualifying corporations from $50 million to $75 million, increasing the statutory formula denominator from $40 million to $60 million above the $15 million threshold.

Concurrently, provincial jurisdictions enacted parallel structural reforms that reshape the sub-national R&D tax environment. British Columbia, acting through Bill 2 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026), and Ontario harmonized their respective provincial R&D tax credits with the federal restoration of capital expenditures and enhanced expenditure thresholds. Meanwhile, Québec enacted a sweeping structural overhaul in its 2025–2026 Budget, abolishing six legacy innovation tax credits and replacing them with a unified refundable tax credit system fostering R&D and pre-commercialization activities, which delivers a 30% refundable credit on the first $1 million of eligible expenditures above an exclusion threshold regardless of corporate asset size, and 20% thereafter.
Statutory and Legislative Foundations of the Federal SR&ED Program
Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1) of the ITA

The legal gateway to all federal and provincial R&D tax incentives in Canada is the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" codified in subsection 248(1) of the ITA, a provision that was relocated to the Act from section 2900 of the Regulations during earlier statutory consolidations. Under subsection 248(1), SR&ED is defined as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that falls within one of four qualifying statutory limbs.

The first limb, codified in paragraph (a) of the definition, encompasses basic research, which is defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view. In commercial corporate tax practice, basic research accounts for a minimal fraction of claims and is predominantly conducted within university laboratories or specialized research institutes. The second limb, set out in paragraph (b), covers applied research, defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view. Applied research frequently arises in early-stage biotechnology, novel cryptographic foundations, quantum computing, and foundational machine learning architecture development. The third and commercially dominant limb, paragraph (c), governs experimental development, which comprises work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto. Experimental development constitutes the vast majority of corporate SR&ED claims in Canada across manufacturing, software engineering, clean technology, and industrial processing. The fourth limb, paragraph (d), incorporates support work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, provided that such work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of core research or experimental development described in paragraphs (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer.

Crucially, even where an activity relates to an innovative commercial project, paragraphs (e) through (k) of the definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) explicitly exclude specific commercial, routine, and non-scientific activities from qualifying either as core SR&ED or as eligible support work.

Applied research: work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view.
Experimental development: work undertaken to achieve technological advancement to create new or improve existing materials, devices, products, or processes.

Engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research commensurate with the needs and directly in support of (a), (b), or (c) performed in Canada.

Market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing; research in the social sciences or humanities; mineral, petroleum, or natural gas prospecting, exploring, drilling, or production; commercial production of new or improved materials, devices, or products or commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; and routine data collection.

body.text: The statutory interplay between paragraph (d) support work and paragraphs (e) through (k) exclusions represents a primary locus of audit adjustments by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA). Computer programming, engineering design, or prototype testing cannot qualify on a standalone basis under paragraph (d); rather, such activities are eligible only to the extent that their volume, duration, and scope are strictly commensurate with the needs of resolving the underlying scientific or technological uncertainty identified under paragraphs (a), (b), or (c). Once the technological uncertainty is resolved and functional or commercial feasibility is demonstrated, all subsequent engineering, debugging, or production activity transitions into excluded commercial production or routine quality control under paragraphs (f) and (i).
The Section 37 Deductible Expenditure Pool

Section 37 of the ITA governs the deductibility of SR&ED expenditures in computing a taxpayer's income from a business carried on in Canada. Rather than subjecting R&D outlays to standard capital expenditure prohibitions under paragraph 18(1)(b) or regular Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) depreciation schedules under paragraph 20(1)(a), subsection 37(1) aggregates eligible domestic SR&ED expenditures into a cumulative, indefinite carryforward pool. Under subsection 37(1), a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may deduct in computing business income for a taxation year an amount not exceeding the positive balance of its SR&ED deductible expenditure pool at the end of that year, or may elect to defer all or part of the deduction to future profitable taxation years indefinitely.

The subsection 37(1) pool is increased each year by three primary expenditure streams. First, subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) adds current expenditures of a revenue nature incurred in the year on SR&ED carried on in Canada directly by the taxpayer. Second, subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.01) through (iii) add eligible payments made to approved associations, universities, colleges, research institutes, or other arm's-length contractors for SR&ED carried on in Canada that is related to a business of the taxpayer. Third, following the enactment of Bill C-15, paragraphs 37(1)(b) and (d) alongside subsection 37(1.2) restore pool additions for capital expenditures incurred on depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, where the property is intended to use all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time over its expected useful life, or consume all or substantially all of its value, in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

Conversely, the subsection 37(1) pool must be reduced by any government assistance or non-government assistance—such as provincial R&D tax credits, forgiveable loans, or direct innovation grants—that the taxpayer has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive at the filing deadline, pursuant to paragraph 37(1)(c) and subsection 127(11.1). Furthermore, the pool is reduced in the current taxation year by the amount of any federal SR&ED ITC claimed as a tax offset or received as a cash refund in the immediately preceding taxation year. Because the federal ITC claimed or refunded in the first year reduces the section 37 deductible expenditure pool in the subsequent year (or triggers a mandatory income inclusion under paragraph 12(1)(t) to the extent that the pool balance would otherwise become negative), the federal SR&ED ITC is effectively brought into taxable income in the following taxation year, preventing a double tax benefit on the same dollar of R&D expenditure.
The Section 127 and 127.1 Investment Tax Credit Regime

While section 37 governs the deduction of R&D outlays in computing net business income, section 127 and section 127.1 of the ITA govern the calculation, utilization, carryback, carryforward, and cash refundability of the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit. Subsection 127(5) permits a taxpayer to deduct its available SR&ED ITCs directly against Part I federal income tax otherwise payable for the taxation year. To the extent that a taxpayer's non-refundable ITCs exceed its Part I tax liability in the year earned, the unused credits may be carried back up to 3 preceding taxation years (limited to the Part I tax remaining payable in those prior years) or carried forward for up to 20 subsequent taxation years.

Subsection 127(9) establishes the core statutory definitions that control ITC computation, including the definitions of "investment tax credit", "qualified expenditure", and "eligible Canadian public corporation". Importantly, subsection 127(9) stipulates that no amount shall be included in a claimant's ITC in respect of an SR&ED expenditure made in the course of earning income if any of the claimant's income is exempt from Part I tax. Subsection 127(10.1) provides the statutory mechanism for the enhanced ITC rate, adding an additional 20% ITC to the baseline 15% ITC—yielding a combined 35% enhanced ITC rate—on qualified expenditures up to the corporation's annual "expenditure limit" for a corporation that qualifies throughout the taxation year either as a CCPC or, for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024, as an ECPC. Finally, section 127.1—operating through subsections 127.1(1), 127.1(2), and 127.1(2.01)—converts unused ITCs earned by eligible claimants into direct cash refunds ("refundable investment tax credits"), which are statutorily deemed under subsection 127(5) to have been applied to reduce Part I tax otherwise payable in the year, thereby extinguishing their availability for future carryforward or carryback.
Federal Rates, Thresholds, Expenditure Caps, and the Bill C-15 Reforms
Evolution from the 2024 Fall Economic Statement to Enacted Bill C-15 (March 26, 2026)

A rigorous statutory audit of Canadian SR&ED claims spanning the 2024, 2025, and 2026 taxation years requires distinguishing carefully between initial policy proposals and the final enacted statute. When the Department of Finance issued the 2024 Fall Economic Statement on December 16, 2024—and subsequently released draft legislative amendments for consultation on August 15, 2025—the government initially proposed increasing the enhanced 35% expenditure limit from $3 million to $4.5 million. However, in Budget 2025 and the resulting implementation legislation, Bill C-15, which received Royal Assent on March 26, 2026, Parliament enacted an even higher annual expenditure limit of $6 million for both CCPCs and ECPCs, retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024.

body.text: A critical compliance nuance governs the transitional boundary of December 16, 2024: eligibility for the $6 million expenditure limit, the $15 million to $75 million phase-out range, and ECPC inclusion depends strictly on the start date of the corporation's taxation year, whereas the restoration of capital expenditures depends on the acquisition date of the depreciable property (or the date lease costs first become payable). Consequently, a corporation with a calendar taxation year beginning January 1, 2025, as well as every corporation filing for a 2026 taxation year, qualifies in full for the $6 million expenditure limit. Conversely, a CCPC with a non-calendar fiscal year running from December 1, 2024 to November 30, 2025 remains subject to the legacy $3 million expenditure limit and the $10 million to $50 million taxable capital phase-out for that entire fiscal period, even though capital property acquired by that same corporation between December 16, 2024 and November 30, 2025 immediately qualifies as an eligible SR&ED capital expenditure.
Mathematical Mechanics of the Expenditure Limit and Phase-Out Formulas
CCPC Taxable Capital Phase-Out Formula (Subsection 127(10.2))

Prior to March 19, 2019, a CCPC's expenditure limit was reduced under a dual-variable formula that penalized both prior-year taxable income (between $500,000 and $800,000) and prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada. Following the federal repeal of the taxable income factor for taxation years ending after March 18, 2019, the expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.2) is governed solely by taxable capital unless the CCPC executes a gross revenue election.
For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a CCPC's annual expenditure limit is calculated according to the statutory formula:

In this formula, the variable A represents the greater of nil and the amount by which the total taxable capital employed in Canada (determined under Part I.3 of the ITA, as referenced in archived Interpretation Bulletin IT-532) of the CCPC and all associated CCPCs (under subsection 127(10.21)) for the immediately preceding taxation year exceeds $15,000,000, capped at $60,000,000—the point at which prior-year taxable capital reaches $75,000,000 and the expenditure limit is reduced to zero. In linear terms, every $1,000,000 of prior-year taxable capital above $15,000,000 cuts the $6,000,000 expenditure limit by $100,000, or $0.10 per dollar of excess taxable capital.

Where a CCPC has a short taxation year of fewer than 365 days, or where a CCPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year while associated in two or more of those taxation years with another CCPC ending in that same calendar year, subsection 127(10.5) (renumbered from former subsection 127(10.6) by Bill C-15) mandates a proration of the expenditure limit based on the ratio of the number of days in the short taxation year to 365. Furthermore, under paragraph 87(2)(j.6) of the ITA, where a new corporation is formed as the result of a statutory amalgamation, it is deemed to be the same corporation as, and a continuation of, each predecessor corporation for the purposes of computing prior-year taxable capital and expenditure limits under subsection 127(10.2). Subsection 127(10.22) and subsection 127(10.23) also provide targeted deeming rules for non-association of corporations in specific venture capital or technical scenarios.
ECPC and Electing CCPC Gross Revenue Phase-Out Formula (Subsections 127(10.6), 127(10.31), and 127(10.32))

Because public corporations frequently carry substantial issued share capital on their balance sheets that reflects historical equity raises rather than operational scale, newly enacted subsection 127(10.6) calculates the expenditure limit for an Eligible Canadian Public Corporation (ECPC) using a three-year average gross revenue test rather than taxable capital employed in Canada.

To qualify as an ECPC under the definition in subsection 127(9), a corporation must satisfy three cumulative statutory criteria throughout the taxation year: first, the corporation must be resident in Canada (a taxable Canadian corporation); second, the corporation must have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (such as the Toronto Stock Exchange, TSX Venture Exchange, NYSE, or NASDAQ) or have validly elected or been designated to be a public corporation; and third, the corporation must not be controlled, directly or indirectly in any manner whatever, by one or more non-resident persons. For an ECPC—or a consolidated group of ECPCs preparing "consolidated financial statements" as defined in subsection 233.8(1) and governed by the sharing and allocation rules in subsections 127(10.61), 127(10.62), 127(10.63), and 127(10.64)—the $6,000,000 expenditure limit phases out on a straight-line basis as the corporation's or consolidated group's average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years rises from $15,000,000 to $75,000,000. If an entity joins or leaves a consolidated ECPC group during the year, the average annual revenue used is that of the consolidated group as reflected in the consolidated financial statements for the year in question, which present the assets, liabilities, income, expenses, and cash flows of the group members as a single economic entity.

Crucially, under subsection 127(10.31) for a standalone CCPC and subsection 127(10.32) for a CCPC that is a member of an associated group, a CCPC may formally elect for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024 to disapply the taxable capital test in subsection 127(10.2) and instead compute its expenditure limit using the ECPC three-year average annual gross revenue formula. Where an associated group of CCPCs makes this election under subsection 127(10.32), the calculation requires aggregating the average annual revenue reflected in the financial statements of every corporation that is a member of the associated group in the taxation year across the preceding three fiscal years, regardless of whether those corporations were associated during the entirety of that three-year lookback period.

This statutory election carries profound second-order strategic implications for capital-intensive Canadian technology, biotechnology, pharmaceutical, and clean-energy ventures. Under the pre-2024 regime, when a pre-revenue CCPC raised a $60 million venture capital or debt financing round, its balance-sheet share capital and indebtedness pushed its taxable capital employed in Canada past the $50 million threshold in the subsequent taxation year, stripping the enterprise of its 35% refundable ITC and dropping it to a 15% non-refundable credit precisely when its R&D burn rate peaked. By electing under subsection 127(10.31) or subsection 127(10.32) to use the three-year average gross revenue metric, a pre-revenue or early-revenue CCPC carrying $60 million or more in balance-sheet capital but generating less than $15 million in average annual revenue preserves 100% of its $6 million expenditure limit and continues to receive up to $2.1 million annually in cash refunds.
Refundability Mechanics and the "Qualifying Corporation" Distinction

The cash refundability of SR&ED ITCs under section 127.1 of the ITA depends on the claimant's legal entity classification, the nature of the expenditure (current versus capital), and whether the expenditures fall within or above the corporation's annual expenditure limit.

body.text: A vital statutory distinction operates between a CCPC that meets the definition of a "qualifying corporation" under subsection 127.1(2) and a CCPC that is neither a qualifying corporation nor an excluded corporation, which is governed by subsection 127.1(2.01). A CCPC is a "qualifying corporation" for a taxation year if its taxable income for the immediately preceding taxation year—combined with the prior-year taxable incomes of all associated corporations—does not exceed its "qualifying income limit". For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, Bill C-15 expanded the qualifying income limit formula to reflect the higher $15 million to $75 million taxable capital corridor:

where A represents the amount by which the associated group's prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15,000,000, causing the qualifying income limit to reach zero when prior-year taxable capital hits $75,000,000 (an expansion from the pre-reform $40,000,000 denominator that phased out between $10 million and $50 million).

If a CCPC's prior-year taxable income exceeds its qualifying income limit—for instance, a profitable CCPC earning $2,000,000 in prior-year taxable income while maintaining $5,000,000 in taxable capital—the corporation ceases to be a "qualifying corporation" under subsection 127.1(2). However, subsection 127.1(2.01) specifically steps in to grant such a CCPC a 100% cash refund on the 35% enhanced ITC earned on current expenditures (and a 40% cash refund on the 35% ITC earned on capital expenditures) within its $6,000,000 expenditure limit. Consequently, the sole financial impact of whether a CCPC qualifies as a "qualifying corporation" under subsection 127.1(2) relates to expenditures incurred above the $6,000,000 expenditure limit: a qualifying corporation receives a 40% cash refund on the 15% basic ITC earned on spending above the limit (worth an extra 6% of cash on excess spending), whereas a CCPC that is not a qualifying corporation, or an ECPC, earns a 0% cash refund on the 15% basic ITC above the limit and must carry those credits back 3 years or forward 20 years to offset Part I tax.
Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs) and Calculation Methodologies

Once an R&D project satisfies the scientific or technological eligibility requirements of subsection 248(1), the claimant must quantify its allowable SR&ED expenditures under section 37 and its "qualified expenditures" under subsection 127(9).
Direct Labour: Regular Employees vs. Specified Employees

Salaries and wages paid to employees who report to a Canadian permanent establishment for time directly engaged in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada—encompassing hands-on technical experimentation, direct technical supervision of R&D staff, and commensurate paragraph 248(1)(d) support work—are 100% includable in the section 37 expenditure pool. General administrative, executive, human resources, legal, marketing, and clerical remuneration is excluded from direct labour and can only be recognized implicitly through the overhead calculation.

To prevent closely held corporations from inflating refundable SR&ED tax credits by paying discretionary year-end bonuses or excessive salaries to owner-managers, the ITA and Regulations enforce strict statutory caps on "specified employees". Under subsection 248(1), a specified employee is an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or who is a specified shareholder owning, directly or indirectly at any time in the taxation year, 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the capital stock of the employer corporation or any related corporation. First, all bonuses, remuneration based on profits, and taxable benefits paid to a specified employee are completely excluded from allowable SR&ED expenditures. Second, the maximum deductible base salary of a specified employee that may be included in the section 37 SR&ED pool is capped at 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under the Canada Pension Plan, prorated by the number of days the individual was employed in the taxation year and shared among associated corporations. Third, when computing the salary base for the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under the Proxy Method, subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8) of the Regulations further restrict each specified employee's includable salary to the lesser of 75% of the specified employee's total eligible salary (excluding bonuses, profit-based remuneration, and taxable benefits, multiplied by the proportion of time spent on SR&ED) and 2.5 times the YMPE, prorated by days employed in the year.

body.text: Overhead Elections: The Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) vs. The Traditional Method

Taxpayers must make an irrevocable annual election on Form T661 to account for SR&ED overhead and indirect supporting expenditures using either the Proxy Method or the Traditional Method. Under the Proxy Method, governed by paragraph (b) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) and subsection 2900(4) of the Regulations, the claimant computes a notional overhead amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—equal to 55% of the eligible SR&ED salary base of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada. As noted above, the salary base to which the 55% PPA rate applies is narrower than gross payroll: for all employees, bonuses, profit-based pay, and taxable benefits are stripped out of the proxy salary base, and specified employees are subject to the additional 75% and 2.5 × YMPE ceilings under subsections 2900(7) and 2900(8). Under the Proxy Method, the PPA is not added to the section 37 deductible pool because the taxpayer already deducts its actual overhead outlays (such as rent, utilities, and general supplies) as ordinary business expenses under section 9 of the ITA; rather, the 55% PPA is added directly to qualified expenditures on Form T661 and Schedule 31 to generate the 35% enhanced or 15% basic ITC. For software, artificial intelligence, and engineering firms whose primary R&D input is technical labour, the Proxy Method almost invariably produces a substantially higher tax credit recovery while eliminating the compliance burden of tracking incremental overhead invoices.

Conversely, under the Traditional Method, no 55% PPA is claimed. Instead, the taxpayer itemizes and claims actual overhead and other expenditures that are both directly related to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada and incremental—meaning the expenditure would not have been incurred but for the performance of the SR&ED work. The Traditional Method is generally advantageous only for capital- or facility-intensive operations with low internal payroll and exceptionally high dedicated utility, specialized consumable, or contract testing costs that exceed 55% of the direct SR&ED salary base.
Subcontractors, Third-Party Payments, and Non-Arm's-Length Rules

Payments to arm's-length Canadian subcontractors for SR&ED performed in Canada on the claimant's behalf are subject to a mandatory 80% statutory inclusion rate when calculating qualified expenditures for ITC purposes under paragraph (a)(ii) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9), which cross-references subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.01) to (iii). While 100% of an eligible arm's-length contract payment is deductible in the section 37 pool, only 80% enters the qualified expenditure base for the federal 35% or 15% ITC. This 80% inclusion factor is a non-negotiable statutory parameter designed to strip out the subcontractor's assumed commercial mark-up and prevent duplicate claims on the same underlying work.

To substantiate an arm's-length subcontractor claim during a CRA review, the claimant must demonstrate that the contractor performed qualifying SR&ED work or commensurate paragraph 248(1)(d) support work physically within Canada, and that the work was performed "on behalf of" the claimant. Work is considered performed on the claimant's behalf where the claimant bears the financial risk of the R&D, directs the technical specifications and investigative approach, owns the resulting intellectual property or technical findings, and ensures the work advances its own technological knowledge rather than merely purchasing an off-the-shelf commercial deliverable from the vendor. Furthermore, under general CRA administrative rules, businesses paying more than $500 in a calendar year for services must issue Form T4A (Statement of Pension, Retirement, Annuity, and Other Income) and maintain executed contracts and detailed invoices breaking down the specific Canadian SR&ED tasks performed. Where SR&ED is subcontracted to a non-arm's-length party (such as an affiliated corporation), the payor cannot claim an ITC on the contract payment itself; instead, the non-arm's-length performer must claim its own underlying direct wages and materials, or the parties must file a joint agreement to transfer the qualified expenditures.
Materials Consumed vs. Materials Transformed and Recapture Rules

Expenditures on tangible materials are 100% includable in both the section 37 pool and section 127 qualified expenditures provided that the materials are either consumed (rendered virtually valueless, scrapped, or destroyed during experimental trials) or transformed (physically integrated into an experimental prototype, pilot plant, or custom test assembly) in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada.

However, if materials transformed during an SR&ED project—or an experimental prototype, custom assembly, or post-December 15, 2024 capital SR&ED asset—are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use, the SR&ED recapture rules in subsections 127(27) through 127(35) of the ITA apply. Upon commercial conversion or disposition, the lesser of the ITC originally earned on the property or materials and the specified percentage (15% or 35%, corresponding to the ITC rate originally claimed) applied to the proceeds of disposition or fair market value at the time of conversion must be added back directly to the taxpayer's Part I federal tax payable (and, in provinces such as Alberta, increases provincial corporate tax otherwise payable).
Restoration of Capital Expenditures and Treatment of Cloud Computing / GPU Infrastructure

From January 1, 2014 until December 15, 2024, capital expenditures—as well as payments for the right to use or lease property that would constitute capital property if owned by the taxpayer—were completely excluded from both section 37 deductibility and section 127 ITC eligibility. Under Bill C-15, Parliament restored the eligibility of capital expenditures for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024, as well as lease costs that first become payable after December 15, 2024.

To qualify under the restored capital expenditure provisions, the depreciable property must be acquired to be used all or substantially all (defined administratively as 90% or more) of its operating time over its expected useful life in the performance of SR&ED in Canada, or to consume all or substantially all (90% or more) of its value in the performance of SR&ED in Canada. The restored capital rules explicitly exclude buildings, land, leasehold interests in land, inventory, and goodwill, with a narrow statutory carve-out preserving eligibility for certain leasehold interests in a building. For qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs within their $6 million expenditure limit, capital expenditures earn the enhanced 35% ITC, of which 40% is refundable in cash (yielding a 14% immediate cash refund and a 21% non-refundable ITC carryforward).

The restoration of capital expenditures has major practical consequences for hardware-intensive R&D, biotechnology, clean technology, and artificial intelligence companies. Specifically, on-premise graphics processing unit (GPU) clusters, high-performance AI servers, laboratory instrumentation, and pilot-scale fabrication equipment acquired after December 15, 2024 now qualify directly for SR&ED ITCs. Conversely, for cloud computing and remote server expenses (such as Amazon Web Services, Microsoft Azure, or Google Cloud Platform instances), standard software-as-a-service (SaaS) subscriptions and general cloud hosting are treated by the CRA as overhead expenses, which are subsumed within the 55% PPA when the Proxy Method is elected. If a taxpayer instead elects the Traditional Method, dedicated cloud compute instances provisioned exclusively for experimental ML model training or scientific simulation may be claimed as "other expenditures" directly related and incremental to the SR&ED project, provided the claimant retains granular metering logs that segregate experimental compute consumption from commercial production or customer-facing hosting.
Governing Authorities, Tax Forms, Filing Procedures, and Statutory Deadlines
Dual-Track Administration by the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA)

The federal SR&ED program is co-administered by the Department of Finance Canada, which formulates legislative tax policy, and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), which processes claims, conducts technical and financial audits, and issues notices of assessment. Within the CRA, SR&ED compliance reviews are executed by two distinct specialist cadres. Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs) are domain scientists, engineers, and computer scientists employed by the CRA to evaluate whether the claimed activities meet the subsection 248(1) definition of SR&ED under the "Why" and "How" criteria, and whether the claimed direct labour and paragraph 248(1)(d) support work are commensurate with the documented technological uncertainties. Financial Reviewers (FRs) are specialized tax auditors who verify T4 payroll summaries, specified employee shareholdings, subcontractor contracts and proof of payment, overhead elections, and government assistance deductions.

The CRA's published service standard aims to process SR&ED claims within 60 to 180 calendar days from the receipt of a complete claim—60 days for claims (refundable or non-refundable) accepted as filed without audit, and 180 days for refundable claims selected for technical and financial review. Furthermore, the CRA administers a voluntary Pre-Claim Consultation and Pre-Claim Approval framework that allows taxpayers to seek an upfront eligibility assessment from the CRA regarding their R&D projects prior to submitting their tax return.
Mandatory Prescribed Tax Forms (2026 Updates)

Pursuant to subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) of the ITA, a taxpayer must file prescribed forms containing prescribed project and financial information to claim SR&ED deductions and ITCs. Following the Royal Assent of Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, the CRA released revised editions of the core SR&ED tax forms in May 2026 to accommodate post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures, ECPC eligibility, and the $6 million expenditure limit.

body.text: The Strict 18-Month Statutory Reporting Deadline (Subsections 37(11) and 127(9)(m))

One of the most rigid statutory bars in Canadian tax administration is the SR&ED reporting deadline codified in subsection 37(11) (governing section 37 pool deductions) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) (governing ITC entitlement). Under these provisions, a taxpayer's SR&ED reporting deadline is exactly 12 months after the taxpayer's income tax return filing due date for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred.

body.text: If a corporate claimant fails to file prescribed Form T661 and Schedule 31—including the mandatory project-level technical descriptions and expenditure line items—on or before the 18-month reporting deadline, subsection 37(11) and paragraph 127(9)(m) permanently bar the unclaimed expenditures from entering the section 37 pool and permanently extinguish the right to earn an ITC on those costs. Unlike general administrative filing deadlines, the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline is a strict statutory condition precedent: neither the CRA nor the Tax Court of Canada has legal authority under the taxpayer relief provisions to grant discretionary extensions, save for extraordinary government-wide statutory deferrals such as the temporary COVID-19 response measures enacted in 2020. Because an SR&ED claim can only be processed once the CRA has received the underlying income tax return, the CRA officially recommends submitting the SR&ED claim concurrently with the T2 return at the 6-month mark, or at least 90 days prior to the 18-month reporting deadline, providing the CRA sufficient time to conduct an initial completeness review and notify the claimant of any missing information before the statutory bar falls.
Provincial and Territorial R&D Tax Credit Regimes and Federal-Provincial Stacking

Every Canadian province (with the exception of Prince Edward Island, which delivers direct innovation rebates rather than a corporate income tax credit) and the Yukon territory provides a statutory R&D tax incentive that stacks with the federal SR&ED program. Apart from Québec (where provincial R&D tax credits are administered independently by Revenu Québec) and Alberta (where the Innovation Employment Grant is administered by Alberta Treasury Board and Finance, Tax and Revenue Administration), all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits are administered directly by the CRA through supplemental schedules filed with the T2 Corporate Income Tax Return.

body.text: Deep-Dive Analysis of Key Provincial Regimes
Québec's 2025–2026 Structural Overhaul (The New CRIC and Modernized TCEB Regimes)

Prior to 2025, Québec operated a complex web of six separate R&D and innovation tax credits: the Tax Credit for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (salary credit), the Tax Credit for University Research and Public Research Centres, the Tax Credit for Private Partnership Pre-Competitive Research, the Tax Credit for Fees and Dues Paid to a Research Consortium, the Tax Credit for Technological Adaptation Services, and the Industrial Design Tax Credit. In the 2025–2026 Québec Budget, the Québec government abolished those fragmented incentives and instituted a unified refundable tax credit regime fostering R&D and pre-commercialization activities (commonly referred to as the CRIC), administered by Revenu Québec (under payment code 15 for SR&ED) and effective for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025.

The new Québec regime introduces three transformative changes for corporations maintaining an establishment and carrying on business in Québec. First, the reform eliminates the historical corporate asset size phase-out: every eligible corporation now earns the enhanced 30% refundable tax credit rate on up to $1,000,000 of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures exceeding the exclusion threshold, regardless of its consolidated worldwide asset size, and a 20% refundable rate on all eligible expenditures beyond that $1,000,000 limit. Second, eligible expenses are broadened beyond direct R&D labour and 50% of arm's-length subcontractor contracts to encompass pre-commercialization activities and capital equipment acquisition costs. Third, the non-creditable exclusion threshold is simplified to equal the greater of $50,000 per corporation or the sum of the individual employee exclusion thresholds—pegged to the basic personal amount under Québec's personal income tax system ($18,571 in 2025)—adjusted in proportion to the time each employee spends on eligible R&D and pre-commercialization activities.

Simultaneously, the 2025–2026 Québec Budget modernized the Tax Credit for the Development of E-Business (TCEB / CDAE). To foster artificial intelligence (AI) companies in Québec, the budget relaxed the 75% IT sector and 50% software activity revenue tests by explicitly adding data processing and hosting activities, while removing legacy maintenance and evolution activities. The TCEB rate structure is gradually rebalancing its 30% total credit from 23% refundable / 7% non-refundable in 2025 to 22% refundable / 8% non-refundable in 2026, 21% / 9% in 2027, and 20% / 10% in 2028, while cutting the credit rates in half starting in 2026 for corporations deriving at least 50% of gross revenue from services provided to related entities for applications used exclusively outside Québec.
British Columbia and Ontario Harmonization with Federal Bill C-15

In British Columbia, the provincial legislature enacted Bill 2 (Budget Measures Implementation Act, 2026), amending Part 6 of the Income Tax Act (B.C.) (detailed in Bulletin CIT 007) to mirror the federal Bill C-15 enhancements for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. Under the amended BC SR&ED Tax Credit (claimed on CRA Form T666 and entered on Line 674 for the refundable credit or Line 659 for the non-refundable credit on Schedule 5), both CCPCs and Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) can now claim the 10% refundable credit on up to $6,000,000 of BC qualified expenditures (doubling the maximum refundable provincial credit to $600,000), subject to the expanded $15 million to $75 million prior-year taxable capital phase-out, with full restoration of capital expenditures on depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024. Active corporate members of a partnership may also claim their proportionate share of the partnership's non-refundable BC SR&ED credit, and corporations may renounce the credit under subsection 100(1) of the British Columbia Income Tax Act.

Similarly, in Ontario, the provincial government confirmed in the 2026 Ontario Economic Outlook and Fiscal Review (Fall Statement) that the federal Bill C-15 expansion—specifically the restoration of capital expenditures on property acquired on or after December 16, 2024—took effect automatically in Ontario on March 26, 2026 for both the 8% refundable Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC) and the 3.5% non-refundable Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC), injecting an estimated $25 million in additional provincial tax relief across 2025–2027.
Alberta's Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) Incremental Mechanics

Alberta's Innovation Employment Grant (IEG), which took effect on January 1, 2021 under sections 26.95 to 26.99 of the Alberta Corporate Tax Act (replacing the former 10% Alberta SR&ED tax credit repealed on December 31, 2019), operates through the corporate tax system via AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29) and Form AT4970, guided by Information Circular IEG-1R5 (updated June 2026). Rather than applying a flat rate, the IEG provides qualified corporations with an 8% refundable payment on eligible Alberta R&D expenditures up to the corporation's "base level of spending"—calculated as the corporation's average qualifying Alberta R&D spending over the immediately preceding two taxation years—and an enhanced 20% refundable payment (8% base plus a 12% incremental addition) on eligible Alberta R&D spending that exceeds that two-year average base level, up to a $4,000,000 annual expenditure ceiling. Consequently, a startup or corporation undertaking R&D in Alberta for the first time has a two-year historical base spending level of zero, entitling it to the full 20% refundable rate on 100% of its eligible first-year Alberta R&D expenditures (up to $800,000 in cash). The filing deadline for the Alberta IEG is 15 months after the corporation's AT1 filing due date (21 months after taxation year-end), and the credit flows directly to Line 129 of the AT1 return.
Mathematical Mechanics of Federal-Provincial Assistance Reduction (Subsection 127(11.1))

Under subsection 127(11.1) of the ITA, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits and grants constitute government assistance that reduces both the federal section 37 expenditure pool and the federal section 127 qualified expenditure base for the taxation year in which the expenditures are incurred. Crucially, however, provincial R&D tax credits reduce the aggregate qualified expenditure pool rather than the underlying direct SR&ED salary base used to compute the federal 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) under Regulation 2900(4).

To illustrate this mechanism, consider a qualifying CCPC electing the Proxy Method that incurs $100,000 in direct non-specified SR&ED salaries in British Columbia. First, the corporation computes its pre-assistance federal qualified expenditures by adding the $55,000 PPA (55% of $100,000) to the $100,000 direct salary, yielding $155,000. Second, the 10% refundable BC SR&ED credit applies to that $155,000 qualified expenditure base, generating a $15,500 provincial cash refund. Third, under subsection 127(11.1), the $15,500 BC credit is deducted as government assistance from the $155,000 federal qualified expenditure pool, leaving $139,500 in net federal qualified expenditures. Fourth, the federal 35% enhanced refundable ITC applies to the $139,500 net base, yielding $48,825 in federal cash. Combining the $15,500 BC refund and the $48,825 federal refund delivers $64,325 in total cash—a 64.33% cash recovery on the $100,000 salary outlay. In provinces with a 15% refundable credit (such as Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, or Yukon) or a 20% incremental grant (Alberta IEG), or under Québec's 30% CRIC regime, combined federal-provincial cash recovery on eligible R&D labour routinely reaches between 62% and 70%.
Judicial Precedents, Case Law, and CRA Administrative Audit Guidelines
The Foundational Five-Question Test: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen (1998)

The cornerstone of Canadian SR&ED jurisprudence is the landmark judgment of Justice Donald Bowman (as he then was) of the Tax Court of Canada in Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Limited v. The Queen, [1998] 3 C.T.C. 2520, 98 D.T.C. 1839 (TCC). Reviewing Information Circular 86-4R3 and applying a purposive statutory interpretation of the SR&ED definition, Justice Bowman established at paragraph 16 of his reasons a five-criterion legal test that remains the binding judicial standard across Canada for distinguishing qualifying SR&ED from routine engineering or standard technical practice.

First, the court asks whether there was a technological risk or uncertainty that could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures. Justice Bowman defined "routine engineering" as the techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field; if the resolution of a technical problem is reasonably predictable using established principles or standard engineering calculations, no technological uncertainty exists. Second, the court examines whether the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulated hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty, a process involving the observation of the subject matter, the identification of the uncertainty, the formulation of a causal hypothesis, the systematic testing of that hypothesis by experiment or analysis, and the formulation of logical conclusions. Third, the court evaluates whether the procedures adopted accorded with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses, as opposed to intuitive trial-and-error or unsystematic tinkering. Fourth, the court determines whether the process resulted in a technological advancement—meaning an advancement in the stock of scientific or technological knowledge, even if the project was commercially unsuccessful or proved that a hypothesized objective was technically unachievable. Fifth, the court verifies whether a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results was kept contemporaneously as the work progressed.
Appellate Affirmation and Evolution of SR&ED Jurisprudence (1998–2026)

Over the nearly three decades following Northwest Hydraulic, the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA) and the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) have consistently affirmed that all five criteria are conjunctive—meaning a taxpayer's failure to satisfy any one of the five questions requires dismissal of the SR&ED appeal.

body.text: In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88, the appellant taxpayer directly challenged the validity of Northwest Hydraulic, arguing that after the definition of SR&ED was relocated from Regulation 2900 to subsection 248(1) of the ITA, the Tax Court Judge erred in requiring adherence to the "scientific method" because the words "scientific method" do not appear in the statutory text of subsection 248(1). Writing for a unanimous Federal Court of Appeal, Justice Wyman W. Webb dismissed the appeal and awarded costs to the Crown, holding that Justice Bowman's five criteria constitute the settled judicial interpretation of the statutory words "systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis", as previously endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie, C.W. Agencies, Jentel Manufacturing, and R&D Pro-Innovation.
The CRA's Two-Pillar ("Why" and "How") Administrative Framework and Software/AI Audit Standards

To align its administrative audit manuals with Northwest Hydraulic and Kam-Press, the CRA archived its legacy Eligibility of Work for SR&ED Investment Tax Credits Policy and structured its current eligibility guidelines around two overarching inquiries. First, under the "Why" requirement, the CRA evaluates whether the work was conducted for the advancement of scientific knowledge or for the purpose of achieving a technological advancement. A technological advancement arises only when existing scientific knowledge or standard engineering practice cannot determine whether a desired objective is achievable (capability uncertainty), how to achieve it within simultaneous system-level constraints (methodology uncertainty), or which structural configuration will satisfy competing technical specifications (design uncertainty). Second, under the "How" requirement, the CRA assesses whether the work was carried out by means of a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis. This requires objective contemporaneous evidence of four steps: formulating a hypothesis (an idea consistent with known facts serving as a starting point for investigation); testing that hypothesis through controlled experimentation or analysis where variables are isolated and measured; developing logical conclusions from the experimental findings; and preserving evidence generated as the work progressed.

In the software development, information technology, and artificial intelligence sectors, CRA Research and Technology Advisors scrutinize claims across three primary qualifying scenarios. In the first scenario, the software itself is the novel technological object, such as developing novel algorithms where no known solution satisfies performance bounds, creating new database storage or query optimization architectures, designing novel machine learning architectures or training methodologies to resolve fundamental failure modes in existing models, or building custom compilers for non-standard target environments. In the second scenario, software is combined with hardware to create a technologically advanced product or process, such as embedded control systems with novel signal processing requirements or custom real-time operating systems where standard implementations fall short. In the third scenario, custom software tooling—such as bespoke simulation environments or novel test harnesses—is engineered specifically to enable or validate another qualifying SR&ED project, even if that internal tooling is never shipped to customers. Conversely, training an established ML model architecture on proprietary corporate datasets, tuning performance using standard profiling tools, implementing existing network protocols, or resolving undocumented vendor API bugs without underlying scientific or technological uncertainty are routinely disallowed as standard software engineering.

To satisfy the contemporaneous documentation requirement during a CRA review, claimants must maintain dated, work-specific records showing what work was done, who performed it, when it was performed, and how the expenditures were calculated. Accepted supporting artefacts include project planning documents, minutes of technical meetings and virtual chat logs, whiteboard diagrams, test protocols, raw experimental data and benchmark results, failed prototypes and scrap records, source-code version control histories, time sheets, activity logs, payroll records, purchase invoices, and accounting ledgers.
Direct R&D Grants, Innovation Ecosystem Programs, and Stacking Optimization

In addition to statutory tax credits administered through the tax return, Canada operates a comprehensive suite of direct non-repayable R&D grants and cost-sharing contributions that can be layered alongside federal and provincial SR&ED credits. The flagship federal direct funding mechanism is the National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), which provides technical advisory services through Industrial Technology Advisors (ITAs) and non-repayable financial contributions covering up to 60% to 80% of internal technical salaries and 50% of contractor expenses for Canadian SMEs (with typical awards ranging from $50,000 to over $1,000,000, and a median for-profit award of $75,000 in jurisdictions such as Alberta), alongside the IP Assist sub-stream supporting intellectual property strategy. Although the federal government announced in December 2023 that NRC IRAP would be integrated into a new crown corporation—the Canada Innovation Corporation (CIC)—by 2026–2027, that transition was subsequently deferred, leaving NRC IRAP operating within the National Research Council through 2026.

Complementing NRC IRAP are collaborative academic-industrial research grants administered by Mitacs (including Mitacs Accelerate and Mitacs AI Advantage, which provide $10,000 to $30,000 per graduate student or postdoctoral internship unit), export R&D co-funding under CanExport Innovation, federal Regional Development Agency programs (PrairiesCan, PacifiCan, FedDev Ontario, CED Québec, and ACOA), and provincial innovation grants such as the Alberta Innovates Venture Development Grant (providing $10,000 to $150,000 at up to 75% cost share for TRL 4–9 technology development, which replaced the former Voucher and Micro Voucher programs on May 29, 2026) and Research Manitoba's Technology Commercialization Program.
The Proxy Method Leverage Effect When Stacking NRC IRAP and SR&ED

When a Canadian CCPC or ECPC stacks an NRC IRAP direct salary grant with federal SR&ED and a provincial R&D tax credit under the Proxy Method, a highly advantageous statutory interaction occurs between subsection 127(11.1) of the ITA and subsection 2900(4) of the Regulations. Because an NRC IRAP contribution constitutes government assistance under subsection 127(11.1), the grant is deducted from the total pool of qualified SR&ED expenditures on Form T661, but it does not reduce the underlying direct SR&ED salary base used to compute the 55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA). Consequently, the claimant earns the 55% notional overhead addition on 100% of the gross eligible SR&ED salary—including the salary portion directly reimbursed by NRC IRAP.

Strategic Conclusions and Audit Risk Mitigation Framework

The enactment of federal Bill C-15 on March 26, 2026, alongside harmonized provincial reforms in British Columbia, Ontario, and Québec, has fundamentally expanded the financial scale and structural accessibility of Canadian R&D tax incentives for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024. To capture the full benefit of these legislative enhancements while insulating claims against CRA and Revenu Québec audit adjustments, corporate claimants and tax advisers should implement five integrated compliance protocols.

First, corporations whose taxation year began on or after December 16, 2024 (including calendar year 2025 filers) that submitted their 2025 T2 return prior to March 26, 2026 under the legacy $3 million expenditure limit, or without claiming post-December 15, 2024 capital expenditures, should immediately prepare and file an amended Form T661 (May 15, 2026 version) and Schedule 31 (May 22, 2026 version) before their 18-month reporting deadline expires under subsections 37(11) and 127(9)(m). Second, venture-backed or asset-heavy CCPCs whose prior-year associated taxable capital employed in Canada exceeds $15 million should quantitatively model whether electing into the ECPC three-year average annual gross revenue phase-out method under subsection 127(10.31) or subsection 127(10.32) preserves a greater share of the $6 million enhanced expenditure limit. Third, claimants acquiring depreciable capital property (such as GPU compute clusters, laboratory apparatus, or pilot machinery) after December 15, 2024 must implement asset-level utilization logs proving that the equipment is intended to be used all or substantially all (90% or more) of its operating time over its expected useful life in Canadian SR&ED, while monitoring subsequent commercial deployment to prevent unexpected ITC recapture under subsections 127(27) to 127(35). Fourth, businesses with operations in Québec must reconfigure their internal job-costing systems for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025 to track pre-commercialization activities and capital equipment alongside R&D wages under the unified 30% / 20% CRIC regime, taking advantage of the removal of the historical corporate asset ceiling. Finally, in light of the Federal Court of Appeal's strict adherence to Northwest Hydraulic in Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen (2021 FCA 88) and the Tax Court's rejection of unsubstantiated software claims in National R&D Inc. v. The Queen (2020 TCC 66), R&D leaders must embed explicit hypothesis formulation, variable isolation, and experimental result logging directly into their contemporaneous engineering workflows so that every project is audit-ready prior to filing.
